questions.q: Vulval hematoma is a laceration of an underlying vessel; m/c cause and arteries involved:
opts: Instrumental delivery (m/c); vulval – internal pudendal artery, vaginal – vaginal artery
Spontaneous labour (m/c); uterine artery
Precipitate labour (m/c); ovarian artery
Episiotomy (m/c); inferior rectal artery
questions.exp: M/c cause instrumental delivery (also precipitate labour, rarely spontaneous); vulval hematoma – internal pudendal artery; vaginal – vaginal artery. (Book p540)

questions.q: Presentation and examination of vulval hematoma:
opts: Excruciating perineal pain with inability to pass urine, and a tense bluish tender swelling of the vulva
A painless soft swelling of the vulva with fever and offensive lochia after the delivery
Painless vaginal bleeding with an open cervical os in the first week after delivery
Pruritus with a watery discharge and superficial dyspareunia in the early puerperium
questions.exp: A vulval haematoma is intensely painful, causes retention of urine and appears as a tense bluish swelling that may extend into the thigh. (Book p540)

questions.q: Conservative management of vulval hematoma consists of:
opts: Ice packs, analgesics, vitals monitoring
Antibiotics and warm compress
Uterotonics and TXA
Vaginal packing
questions.exp: Conservative: ice packs, analgesics, monitoring of vitals. (Book p540)

questions.q: Indications for surgical management (incision & drainage with mattress-suture cavity closure):
opts: Larger than 5 cm, still enlarging, excruciating pain, or associated shock
Any haematoma at all that measures more than 1 cm across
Only once the haematoma has become clinically infected
Only when haematomas are present on both sides of the vulva
questions.exp: Surgical drainage is for a large, expanding or very painful collection, or one that has caused shock; small stable ones are managed conservatively. (Book p540)

questions.q: Broad ligament hematoma presents as ______ and is due to ______.
opts: Shock with little visible bleeding; from a cervical or vaginal tear extending upwards
Heavy vaginal bleeding from uterine atony after the delivery
Fever and pelvic pain from puerperal endometritis
A visible vulval swelling from a torn pudendal artery
questions.exp: A supralevator collection is occult: shock out of proportion to visible loss, from an upward extension of a cervical or vaginal tear. (Book p540)

questions.q: Match the puerperal haematoma with its presentation — 1) Vulval haematoma 2) Infralevator vaginal or perineal haematoma 3) Supralevator or broad ligament haematoma … A) A tense, exquisitely tender swelling of the vulva that may extend into the thigh B) A swelling contained below the levator ani, seen as a bluish vaginal or perineal mass C) Occult blood above the levator ani that pushes the uterus up and to one side, sometimes with shock
questions.exp: Infralevator haematomas are visible; supralevator collections are occult and present late with shock out of proportion to visible loss. (Book p540)

questions.q: Match the degree of perineal tear to structures – 1st : 2nd : 3rd : 4th.
opts: Vaginal mucosa : 1 + muscles : 2 + anal sphincter : 3 + rectal mucosa
Skin : mucosa : muscles : sphincter
Mucosa : sphincter : rectum : bladder
Muscles : mucosa : rectal mucosa : sphincter
questions.exp: 1° vaginal mucosa; 2° + perineal muscles; 3° + anal sphincter; 4° + rectal mucosa. (Book p541)

questions.q: Sub-classification of third-degree tear – 3A : 3B : 3C.
opts: <50% of external anal sphincter : ≥50% of EAS : internal and external anal sphincter
≥50% EAS : <50% EAS : IAS only
IAS : EAS : rectal mucosa
EAS partial : rectal mucosa : IAS
questions.exp: 3A <50% EAS; 3B ≥50% EAS; 3C both IAS and EAS (3rd & 4th = complete perineal tear). (Book p541)

questions.q: Repair setting – 1st & 2nd degree : 3rd & 4th degree; suture material:
opts: Labour room under local anaesthesia, like episiotomy : OT under general/spinal anaesthesia; Vicryl for both
OT under GA : labour room under LA; catgut
Bedside without anaesthesia : OT under LA; silk
Both in OT; nylon
questions.exp: 1°/2°: labour room, LA, like episiotomy; 3°/4°: OT under GA/spinal; Vicryl. (Book p541)

questions.q: Sequence of repair for 1st/2nd degree tear:
opts: Vaginal mucosa continuous sutures → muscles interrupted sutures → vaginal skin mattress sutures
Skin → muscles → mucosa
Muscles interrupted → mucosa mattress → skin continuous
Mucosa mattress → skin interrupted → muscles continuous
questions.exp: Mucosa continuous, muscles interrupted, skin mattress. (Book p541)

questions.q: Sequence of repair for 3rd/4th degree tear:
opts: Rectal mucosa → internal anal sphincter → external anal sphincter (end-to-end anastomosis) → rest like episiotomy
External sphincter → rectal mucosa → internal sphincter
Vaginal mucosa → EAS → rectal mucosa
Skin → IAS → EAS → mucosa
questions.exp: Rectal mucosa, IAS, EAS end-to-end, then like episiotomy. (Book p541)

questions.q: Timing of perineal tear repair – <24 h of delivery : >24 h of delivery.
opts: Immediate repair : repair after minimum 3 weeks
Repair after 3 weeks : immediate
Immediate : after 6 months
Both immediate
questions.exp: <24 h immediate; >24 h wait minimum 3 weeks. (Book p541)

questions.q: WHO recommendations to PREVENT perineal tear include all EXCEPT:
opts: Fundal massage / routine episiotomy
Perineal massage and warm compression
Controlled delivery of fetal head and guarding of perineum
Ritgen manoeuvre
questions.exp: Fundal massage and routine episiotomy are NOT recommended. (Book p541)

questions.q: Fill up: A second-degree perineal tear involves the ______, whereas a third-degree tear involves the ______.
opts: perineal muscles; anal sphincter complex
skin only; perineal muscles
anal sphincter; anal mucosa
vaginal mucosa alone; the perineal body
questions.exp: Third- and fourth-degree tears extend into, or through, the anal sphincter and mucosa and must be repaired by an experienced operator in theatre. (Book p541)

questions.q: Episiotomy is a surgically planned incision of the perineum to facilitate delivery of the fetal head; indications include:
opts: Shoulder dystocia, instrumental delivery, the after-coming head of a breech and a rigid perineum
Every primigravida, to shorten the second stage and protect the pelvic floor
Every preterm delivery, to reduce intracranial haemorrhage in the preterm baby
Every twin pregnancy routinely, whatever the presentation or progress of labour
questions.exp: Episiotomy is a selective, not routine, procedure; the listed indications all need a rapid or atraumatic delivery. (Book p541)

questions.q: Types of episiotomy – median : mediolateral.
opts: At centre extending from introitus : at an angle of 60°
At 45° : at centre
Lateral from 3 o'clock : J-shaped
questions.exp: Median from introitus at centre; mediolateral at 60°. (Book p542)

questions.q: Correct timing of episiotomy:
opts: After crowning; climbing of perineum in breech; before/after forceps application but before traction
Before crowning
At full dilatation regardless of descent
After delivery of head
questions.exp: After crowning; in breech when perineum is 'climbed'; with forceps before traction. (Book p542)

questions.q: Median vs mediolateral episiotomy – muscle fibres cut, bleeding, repair, healing:
opts: Median: less fibres, less bleeding, easy repair, quick healing; mediolateral: more, more, difficult, longer
Median: more, more, difficult, longer; mediolateral: less, less, easy, quick
Both equal
Median: less fibres but more bleeding
questions.exp: Median cuts fewer fibres, bleeds less, repairs easily and heals quickly; mediolateral the opposite. (Book p542)

questions.q: Median vs mediolateral – chance of gaping, dyspareunia and anal sphincter involvement:
opts: Median: ↓ gaping, ↓ dyspareunia but anal sphincter involved; mediolateral: ↑ gaping, ↑ dyspareunia, sphincter not involved
Median: ↑ gaping, sphincter spared; mediolateral: ↓ gaping, sphincter involved
Both involve sphincter
Neither involves sphincter
questions.exp: Median: less gaping/dyspareunia, but risk of anal sphincter extension; mediolateral: more gaping/dyspareunia, sphincter spared. (Book p542)

questions.q: Structures cut in an episiotomy:
opts: Vaginal mucosa, skin and subcutaneous tissue, the superficial perineal muscles and pudendal branches
The anal sphincter and the rectal mucosa, as in a fourth-degree tear
The levator ani muscle alone, with no skin or mucosal tissue
Bartholin's gland and the urethra, which lie within the incision line
questions.exp: An episiotomy cuts vaginal mucosa, skin and subcutaneous tissue, the perineal muscles and branches of the pudendal vessels and nerve. (Book p542)

questions.q: Muscles CUT vs NOT cut in episiotomy:
opts: Cut: pubococcygeus, deep & superficial transverse perinei, bulbospongiosus; not cut: ischiocavernosus, ischiococcygeus, obturator, anal sphincter
Cut: ischiocavernosus, anal sphincter; not cut: bulbospongiosus
Cut: obturator internus; not cut: pubococcygeus
Cut: anal sphincter; not cut: transverse perinei
questions.exp: Cut: pubococcygeus, deep/superficial transverse perinei, bulbospongiosus. Spared: ischiocavernosus, ischiococcygeus, obturator, anal sphincter. (Book p542)

questions.q: Episiotomy scissors are identified by:
opts: Rounded ends and an angulated blade
Sharp pointed ends and straight blade
Serrated jaws with ratchet
Curved blunt-tipped blades with teeth
questions.exp: Episiotomy scissors: rounded ends, angulated. (Book p542)

questions.q: All of the following statements about a mediolateral episiotomy are true EXCEPT:
opts: It is cut straight backwards in the midline to minimise bleeding
It is angled about 45 to 60 degrees away from the midline
It lowers the risk of extension into the anal sphincter compared with a midline cut
It bleeds more and is more painful afterwards than a midline episiotomy
questions.exp: A midline cut is the one made straight backwards; the mediolateral cut is angled away from the sphincter, which is why it is safer. (Book p542)

questions.q: Malposition is defined by longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation, vertex presenting part and position:
opts: Any position other than 1–5 (i.e., ROP 6, DOP 7, LOP 8)
Any position other than DOA
Positions 1–5
LOT and ROT only
questions.exp: Malposition = OP positions 6 (ROP), 7 (DOP), 8 (LOP). (Book p543)

questions.q: Most common OP positions in order and the causes:
opts: ROP (6) > DOP (7) > LOP (8); android pelvis (m/c – head occupies posterior part due to ↑ space) > deflexed head
LOP > DOP > ROP; anthropoid pelvis > macrosomia
DOP > ROP > LOP; platypelloid pelvis
LOP > ROP > DOP; gynaecoid pelvis
questions.exp: ROP > DOP > LOP; causes android pelvis (m/c) then deflexed head. (Book p543)

questions.q: Incidence of OP position at term/onset of labour vs late labour, and parity associations:
opts: About 10% at the onset of labour falling to about 2% as most rotate; malposition is commoner in nulliparous women
About 2% at the onset rising to about 10%, and commoner in multiparous women throughout
About 25% at the onset falling to about 5%, and commoner in nulliparous women throughout
About 10% throughout labour, with no association with parity at all
questions.exp: Most occipito-posterior heads rotate spontaneously, so the incidence falls from about 10% to about 2%; the malposition is commoner in nulliparas. (Book p543)

questions.q: Abdominal findings — occipito-posterior : occipito-anterior.
opts: OP: flat lower abdomen, limbs near the midline, heart in the flank — OA: convex abdomen with the limbs behind
OP: convex abdomen with the limbs behind — OA: flat lower abdomen, limbs near the midline, heart in the flank
OP: heart loudest in the midline — OA: heart in the flank with a flat lower abdomen below the umbilicus
OP: limbs in the flank with the heart in the midline — OA: bulging flanks with limbs felt on both sides
questions.exp: In occipito-posterior the deflexed head leaves the lower abdomen flat, brings the limbs forwards and pushes the fetal heart out to the flank. (Book p544)

questions.q: Engaging diameters – OP (deflexed head) : OA (well flexed head).
opts: Occipitofrontal 11.5 cm / suboccipitofrontal 10 cm with delayed engagement : suboccipitobregmatic 9.5 cm
Suboccipitobregmatic 9.5 cm : occipitofrontal 11.5 cm
Mentovertical 14 cm : submentobregmatic 9.5 cm
Biparietal 9.5 cm : bitemporal 8 cm
questions.exp: OP engages by occipitofrontal 11.5 cm/suboccipitofrontal 10 cm (delayed); OA by suboccipitobregmatic 9.5 cm. (Book p544)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about occipito-posterior position is TRUE?
opts: The anterior fontanelle is easily felt, the head is deflexed and labours are longer with severe backache
The sagittal suture lies in the transverse diameter and always rotates posteriorly
Vaginal delivery is impossible, so caesarean section is always required
The position is linked to the anthropoid pelvis but never to the android pelvis
questions.exp: Deflexion presents a larger diameter, so labour is longer and backache is prominent; most rotate anteriorly or deliver face-to-pubis. (Book p544)

questions.sec: Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
questions.q: Three possible outcomes in OP position and the m/c one:
opts: Complete forward rotation, which is commonest; incomplete forward rotation; and persistent posterior rotation
Persistent posterior rotation, which is commonest; complete forward rotation; and deep sacral arrest
Incomplete forward rotation, which is commonest; complete forward rotation; and face-to-pubis delivery
Deep sacral arrest, which is commonest; complete forward rotation; and persistent posterior rotation
questions.exp: Most occipito-posterior heads rotate forwards completely to occipito-anterior; the rest rotate incompletely or persist as occipito-posterior. (Book p544)

questions.sec: Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
questions.q: Incomplete forward rotation – rotation achieved and causes:
opts: Only 1/8th rotation (ROP → ROT); android pelvis (m/c), big baby, ↓ liquor
2/8th rotation; anthropoid pelvis
3/8th rotation; platypelloid pelvis
No rotation; polyhydramnios
questions.exp: Only 1/8th rotation to OT; causes android pelvis (m/c), big baby, oligohydramnios. (Book p545)

questions.sec: Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
questions.q: Deep transverse arrest is defined as:
opts: The head stuck in the occipito-transverse position at the spines despite adequate contractions, usually with an android pelvis
The head arrested at the pelvic brim in the occipito-posterior position
The head arrested at the outlet in the occipito-anterior position
A face presentation arrested in the persistent mento-posterior position
questions.exp: Deep transverse arrest is failure of internal rotation from the transverse position at the level of the ischial spines. (Book p545)

questions.sec: Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
questions.q: Management of deep transverse arrest — android pelvis : roomy pelvis.
opts: Android pelvis: caesarean section — roomy pelvis: manual or Kielland rotation followed by instrumental delivery
Android pelvis: manual rotation then forceps — roomy pelvis: caesarean section without a trial of rotation
Both android and roomy pelvis: caesarean section in every case, since rotation is never successful
Both android and roomy pelvis: vacuum extraction as the first-line treatment in the second stage
questions.exp: Rotation then instrumental delivery is reasonable only when the pelvis is roomy; with an android pelvis caesarean is safer. (Book p545)

questions.sec: Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
questions.q: Posterior rotation (ROP → DOP) is most commonly seen with:
opts: Anthropoid pelvis (AP diameter >> transverse)
Android pelvis
Platypelloid pelvis
Gynaecoid pelvis
questions.exp: Posterior rotation is m/c in anthropoid pelvis (AP >> transverse). (Book p545)

questions.sec: Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
questions.q: In the second stage the head is at station +2 in the occipito-transverse position after an hour of pushing, with good contractions, a normal pelvis and a normal CTG. What is the management?
opts: Manual rotation to occipito-anterior, then instrumental delivery, or rotational forceps by an experienced operator; caesarean if these fail
Continue pushing for another two hours without intervention
Immediate caesarean section without attempting rotation
Symphysiotomy, because rotation is never appropriate in the second stage
questions.exp: Persistent occipito-transverse arrest can be resolved by manual or instrumental rotation when the pelvis is adequate and the operator is trained. (Book p545)

questions.sec: Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
questions.q: Outcome of posterior rotation — anthropoid pelvis : other pelvis types.
opts: Anthropoid: face-to-pubes delivery — other pelvis: deep sacral arrest with the head stuck
Anthropoid: deep sacral arrest — other pelvis: face-to-pubes delivery
Both pelves end in a face-to-pubes delivery after posterior rotation
Both pelves require caesarean section once rotation has gone posterior
questions.exp: The long antero-posterior diameter of the anthropoid pelvis permits face-to-pubes delivery; in other pelves the head arrests deeply. (Book p546)

questions.sec: Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
questions.q: The m/c complication of face-to-pubes delivery and its implication:
opts: Complete perineal tear – hence an indication for episiotomy
Shoulder dystocia – McRoberts
Cord prolapse – C-section
PPH – oxytocin
questions.exp: Face-to-pubes → complete perineal tear → episiotomy indicated. (Book p546)

questions.q: Transverse lie – presentation : denominator : m/c position.
opts: Shoulder : acromion process : dorso-anterior > dorso-posterior
Shoulder : scapula : dorso-posterior
Arm : acromion : dorso-superior
Breech : sacrum : sacro-anterior
questions.exp: Shoulder presentation, denominator acromion, dorso-anterior m/c. (Book p546)

questions.q: M/c outcome and causes of transverse lie:
opts: Spontaneous rotation >34 weeks to cephalic/breech; m/c cause overall prematurity, at term placenta previa
Persistent transverse lie; m/c cause fibroid
Cord prolapse; m/c cause twins
Obstructed labour; m/c cause CPD
questions.exp: Usually rotates after 34 wks; m/c cause overall prematurity, at term placenta previa. (Book p546)

questions.q: Examination and complication of transverse lie:
opts: Uterine height < period of gestation; fundal and deep pelvic grips empty; highest chance of cord prolapse (cervix not closed by head)
Height > POG; fundus contains head; shoulder dystocia
Height = POG; pelvic grip head; PPH
Fundus buttocks; face presentation
questions.exp: Fundal height less than dates, empty fundal and pelvic grips; highest cord prolapse risk. (Book p546)

questions.q: Fill up: A transverse lie at term with a live fetus is delivered by ______, and the gravest complication of a neglected case is ______.
opts: caesarean section; rupture of the uterus
internal podalic version; cord prolapse
external cephalic version; placental abruption
forceps delivery; cervical laceration
questions.exp: Neglected shoulder presentation stretches the lower segment until it ruptures; delivery is by caesarean section once the lie persists at term. (Book p547)

questions.q: Indications for caesarean section in transverse lie (no mechanism of labour):
opts: Two failed attempts at version, version contraindicated, or transverse lie in active labour
Only when the fetus is known to be alive at the time of diagnosis
Only in a primigravida with an unscarred uterus
Only once the membranes have ruptured spontaneously in labour
questions.exp: A transverse lie at term is delivered by caesarean when version fails or is contraindicated, or once labour is established. (Book p548)

questions.q: Hand prolapse/neglected shoulder presentation – pathophysiology and management:
opts: A vaginal delivery is attempted, the hand is pulled to rotate, obstructed labour with Bandl's ring follows, and caesarean is needed
The lie corrects spontaneously and internal podalic version delivers the fetus vaginally
Cord prolapse occurs first and forceps are applied to the after-coming head
The fetus converts to a breech, and breech extraction with decapitation is then performed
questions.exp: Neglected shoulder presentation is iatrogenic: traction on the prolapsed hand obstructs labour, and delivery must be by caesarean. (Book p548)

questions.q: Indications for ECV and preliminary USG confirmations:
opts: Breech and transverse lie, with ultrasound confirming lie, liquor, singleton pregnancy and no gross anomaly
Face and brow presentation, with ultrasound assessing the placenta alone
Twin pregnancy, with ultrasound determining chorionicity and amnionicity
Occipito-posterior position, with ultrasound measuring the biparietal diameter
questions.exp: Version is offered for breech and transverse lie after ultrasound confirms the lie, adequate liquor, a singleton and no major anomaly. (Book p546)

questions.q: ECV procedure details:
opts: Outpatient, no anaesthesia, terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously, anti-D if Rh-negative, continuous monitoring
An inpatient procedure under general anaesthesia with no tocolysis, followed by induction
In theatre under spinal anaesthesia with nifedipine, always followed by induction
An outpatient procedure under epidural analgesia with no fetal monitoring
questions.exp: Version is done as an outpatient with tocolysis, anti-D cover and continuous monitoring, and without routine anaesthesia or induction. (Book p547)

questions.q: If fetal distress occurs during ECV:
opts: Stop at once, turn the baby back to its original position, and proceed to caesarean section
Continue the version quickly so that the procedure can be completed
Give oxytocin and deliver the baby vaginally as soon as possible
Wait thirty minutes for the trace to recover and then try again
questions.exp: Fetal distress during version means abandoning the procedure, reverting the presentation, and delivering by caesarean section. (Book p547)

questions.q: Pre-requisites for ECV include all EXCEPT:
opts: Ruptured membranes
Gestation ≥36 weeks (m/c done at 37 weeks – less reversion) and adequate liquor
Singleton pregnancy with normal CTG
Can be done in latent phase; no contraindication to vaginal delivery
questions.exp: Prerequisites: ≥36 wks (37 usual), adequate liquor, INTACT membranes, early labour ok, singleton, normal FHR, no C/I to vaginal delivery. (Book p547)

questions.q: Relative contraindications to ECV:
opts: PIH, maternal heart disease, IUGR, previous LSCS
Oligohydramnios, ruptured membranes
Twins, placenta previa
Abnormal CTG, gross anomalies
questions.exp: Relative: PIH, heart disease, IUGR, previous LSCS. (Book p547)

questions.q: Absolute contraindications to ECV include:
opts: Ruptured membranes, oligohydramnios, placenta previa, an abnormal cardiotocograph or a uterine scar
Pregnancy-induced hypertension, fetal growth restriction and mild iron deficiency anaemia
One previous lower segment caesarean section and well-controlled maternal heart disease
A gestation of 36 weeks, an anterior placenta and a maternal age above thirty-five years
questions.exp: Absolute contraindications make version unsafe; a previous lower segment caesarean and 36 weeks are relative considerations, not absolute bars. (Book p547)

questions.q: ECV attempt outcomes – successful 1st attempt : fails 1st attempt → retry another day; successful 2nd : fails 2nd.
opts: Wait for spontaneous labour (do not induce) : induce with oxytocin drip : elective caesarean at 39 weeks
Induce immediately : wait : C-section at 37 weeks
C-section : wait : induce
Wait : wait : third attempt
questions.exp: 1st success → await spontaneous labour; 2nd success → induce with oxytocin; 2nd failure → elective C-section at 39 wks. (Book p547)

questions.q: All of the following are contraindications to external cephalic version EXCEPT:
opts: An uncomplicated breech at 37 weeks with normal liquor volume and a reassuring CTG
Placenta previa or an anterior placenta low in the uterus
Ruptured membranes with reduced liquor volume
A non-reassuring fetal heart rate pattern before the procedure
questions.exp: An uncomplicated breech at term is exactly the indication for external cephalic version, which is offered with tocolysis after a reassuring trace. (Book p547)

questions.q: Face presentation – lie, presentation, presenting part, attitude, denominator:
opts: Longitudinal; cephalic; face; complete extension (abnormal attitude); mentum
Longitudinal; cephalic; brow; partial extension; frontal bone
Transverse; shoulder; face; flexion; acromion
Longitudinal; breech; face; extension; sacrum
questions.exp: Face: longitudinal lie, cephalic, face presenting, complete extension, denominator mentum. (Book p548)

questions.q: Risk factors for face presentation:
opts: Anencephaly, anything preventing flexion such as a tight cord, and a roomy multiparous uterus
Hydrocephalus, a primigravid uterus and an android pelvis
Oligohydramnios with fetal growth restriction in a primigravida
Placenta previa with a gynaecoid pelvis and a well-flexed head
questions.exp: Face presentation needs extension: anencephaly, a nuchal cord or neck mass that blocks flexion, and a lax multiparous uterus. (Book p548)

questions.q: Positions in face presentation – m/c position and engaging diameter:
opts: Left mento-anterior; submento-bregmatic 9.5 cm
Right mento-posterior; mento-vertical 14 cm
Mento-transverse; occipito-frontal 11.5 cm
Direct mento-posterior; biparietal
questions.exp: LMA is m/c; engaging diameter submento-bregmatic 9.5 cm (positions: mento-posterior, mento-anterior, mento-transverse). (Book p549)

questions.q: Management — mento-anterior : mento-posterior.
opts: Mento-anterior: vaginal delivery once the chin rotates forward — mento-posterior: caesarean, since no mechanism exists
Mento-anterior: caesarean section in every case — mento-posterior: vaginal delivery after manual rotation
Both mento-anterior and mento-posterior: caesarean section without any trial of labour
Both mento-anterior and mento-posterior: a trial of forceps from the pelvic floor
questions.exp: Mento-anterior can deliver vaginally once the chin is to the front; persistent mento-posterior has no mechanism of labour and needs caesarean section. (Book p549)

questions.q: In which situations is the head delivered by FLEXION, and where is C-section mandatory?
opts: Flexion in breech and face presentation; caesarean for transverse lie, mento-posterior face and brow
Flexion in vertex presentation; caesarean for a persistent occipito-posterior position
Flexion in brow presentation; caesarean for a left mento-anterior face presentation
Flexion in every presentation, with caesarean section never actually mandatory
questions.exp: Breech and face deliver by flexion; transverse lie, persistent mento-posterior and brow presentation cannot deliver vaginally. (Book p549)

questions.q: Match the malpresentation with its outcome — 1) Mento-anterior face presentation 2) Mento-posterior face presentation 3) Brow presentation … A) Presents the largest diameter of the fetal head, so spontaneous vaginal delivery is not possible B) Can deliver vaginally once the chin rotates to the front and the head flexes under the symphysis C) Cannot deliver vaginally, because the head cannot flex further in the cavity
questions.exp: Mento-anterior can deliver vaginally, a persistent mento-posterior cannot, and brow presents the mento-vertical diameter of about 13.5 cm. (Book p549)

questions.q: Brow presentation occurs in ______ and the bony landmarks felt on P/V are ______.
opts: Partial extension of head; anterior fontanelle (diamond) and supraorbital ridges
Complete extension; mentum and nose
Complete flexion; posterior fontanelle
Deflexion; both fontanelles
questions.exp: Brow = partial extension; P/V feels anterior fontanelle and supraorbital ridges. (Book p549)

questions.q: Engaging diameter and denominator in brow presentation:
opts: Mento-vertical 14 cm; frontal bone
Submento-bregmatic 9.5 cm; mentum
Occipito-frontal 11.5 cm; occiput
Suboccipito-bregmatic 9.5 cm; sinciput
questions.exp: Mento-vertical 14 cm; denominator frontal bone. (Book p549)

questions.q: Management of brow presentation:
opts: No mechanism of labour → only C-section; in early labour wait & watch since complete extension (face) or flexion (vertex) may occur
Forceps delivery
Vacuum extraction
Manual conversion to face then vaginal delivery always
questions.exp: Brow → C-section; early labour may convert to face or vertex. (Book p549)

questions.q: Fill up: The presenting diameter in brow presentation is the ______, which measures about ______ cm.
opts: mento-vertical; 13.5
submento-bregmatic; 9.5
occipito-frontal; 11.5
suboccipito-bregmatic; 9.5
questions.exp: The partially extended head presents the mento-vertical diameter of 13.5 cm, the largest that the fetal head can offer, so it cannot negotiate a normal pelvis. (Book p549)

units.title: Vulval hematoma & broad ligament hematoma
units.guide: Identify the artery, cause and presentation of vulval hematoma, decide between conservative and surgical care, and recognise the hidden broad-ligament bleed. Focus for this checkpoint: Vulval hematoma & broad ligament hematoma.

units.title: Perineal tear: classification & repair
units.guide: Grade perineal tears including the 3A/3B/3C subdivisions, and sequence the repair by degree, setting, suture and timing. Focus for this checkpoint: Perineal tear: classification & repair.

units.title: Episiotomy: indications, types, timing & anatomy
units.guide: List the indications, compare median with mediolateral episiotomy feature by feature, know the correct moment to cut and which muscles are divided. Focus for this checkpoint: Episiotomy: indications, types, timing & anatomy.

units.title: Occipito-posterior malposition: features, causes & findings
units.guide: Define malposition, rank the OP positions and causes, and contrast OP with OA on abdominal findings and engaging diameters. Focus for this checkpoint: Occipito-posterior malposition: features, causes & findings.

units.title: Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
units.guide: Work through complete forward rotation, incomplete rotation with deep transverse arrest, and posterior rotation with face-to-pubes delivery. Focus for this checkpoint: Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest.

units.title: Transverse lie & shoulder presentation
units.guide: Characterise transverse lie by denominator, position, causes and examination, know its cord-prolapse risk and the C-section-only rules including neglected shoulder. Focus for this checkpoint: Transverse lie & shoulder presentation.

units.title: External cephalic version (ECV)
units.guide: Prepare for ECV with the right prerequisites and USG checks, know its procedure, contraindications and what to do after success or failure. Focus for this checkpoint: External cephalic version (ECV).

units.title: Face presentation
units.guide: Describe face presentation's attitude and denominator, its risk factors, positions with the m/c one, and management by mento-anterior vs mento-posterior. Focus for this checkpoint: Face presentation.

units.title: Brow presentation
units.guide: Recognise brow presentation by its landmarks and 14 cm diameter, and know why it can only deliver by C-section unless it converts. Focus for this checkpoint: Brow presentation.
